title: David Suchet Reveals the 1 Reason He Is the Best Hercule Poirot
metaDescription: David Suchet Hercule Poirot fans still debate who wore the moustache best. Here is why the late actor's 25-year run remains the gold standard.
author: EpisodeLens Staff
altText: David Suchet as Hercule Poirot in the classic Agatha Christie TV series, wearing a suit and bow tie
html:
David Suchet Hercule Poirot is a name that still sparks fierce debate among mystery lovers. The English actor played Agatha Christie's fussy Belgian detective for a quarter of a century, and for many viewers, no one else comes close. That question, simple as it sounds, cuts to the heart of why one performance can define a character for a whole generation.

Why David Suchet Hercule Poirot Still Feels Untouchable

Suchet took on the role in 1989 for the ITV series Agatha Christie's Poirot. He kept it until the final episode aired in 2013, which means he lived inside the character for nearly 25 years. That kind of run is rare for any actor, let alone one playing a single detective across dozens of stories.

Fans often point to the small things. The walk. The precise way he straightened his tie. The obsessive neatness that somehow made Poirot both funny and sad. Suchet studied the books closely and built the character from the page up, which is why so many readers say he looks exactly like the man they imagined.

Other actors have played Poirot, including Peter Ustinov and Kenneth Branagh. Each brought something different. Ustinov leaned into charm. Branagh went big and theatrical. Suchet went quiet and exact, and that contrast is why the debate never really dies.

From Stage Actor to TV Detective

Before Poirot, Suchet built a serious stage career in London. He trained at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art and worked steadily in theatre, film, and television. He also played roles as varied as Shakespeare's villains and real historical figures, so the detective was never his only identity.

Still, the moustache followed him everywhere. He spoke openly about how the role changed his life and how protective he felt about getting it right. He once described the pressure of playing a character so many people already loved in their heads, which is a burden few actors ever face.

That care shows on screen. Even in weaker episodes, Suchet never phones it in. He treats every case like it matters, and that consistency is what turned a TV detective into a cultural touchstone.

What Makes a Great Poirot

Agatha Christie wrote Poirot as a fussy, foreign outsider in English society. He notices everything. He trusts his little grey cells. He is vain, kind, and occasionally cruel in his honesty. A bad performance makes him a cartoon. A great one makes him human.

Suchet found the humanity. He let Poirot be ridiculous and brilliant at the same time. He also aged with the character, which gave the later stories real weight. By the final season, you could feel the years in his voice, and that made the ending hit harder.

Why the Debate Keeps Going

New adaptations keep arriving, so new fans keep discovering the character. Some fall for Branagh's blockbuster version. Others go back to Suchet and stay there. That is not a knock on anyone else. It just shows how strong his foundation was.

There is also the sheer volume of work. Suchet filmed 70 episodes across 13 series, covering almost every Poirot story Christie wrote. No other actor has come close to that total. Quantity alone does not make you the best, but combined with quality, it makes a strong case.

The Verdict on the Best Poirot

So, do you think David Suchet Hercule Poirot is the best of all time? For a lot of viewers, the answer is an easy yes. He gave the character time, respect, and a strange kind of warmth that is hard to copy. He made a Belgian detective feel like an old friend.

Others will always prefer a different take, and that is fine. Great characters can hold more than one great performance. But when people picture Poirot, most of them still see Suchet, and that image is not going anywhere soon.

Drop your pick in the comments. Who wore the moustache best?
